newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Investors turn backs on puny yields.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Investors turn backs on puny yields.

text.p: Global bond market euphoria sent debt prices to record levels last week, but as investors grow uneasy about such low yields the risks of a correction are mounting, analysts said on Monday.
Changing expectations of European interest rates pushed benchmark Bund yields near to historic lows, while key technical levels were broken on most bond futures contracts.
"With (10-year) Bund yields at 5.6 percent, investors are reluctant to chase yields much lower," said Philip Tyson, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London.
"The lond end of Europe is going to find progress increasingly difficult," he said.

Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago in London, said German benchmark yields would hit resistance at 5.5 percent, as all but the most speculative investors would drop out of the game.

He said the yield on the U.S. long bond would have trouble at the 6.25 percent barrier, compared with a current level of about 6.38 percent. Japanese bonds, too, were in uncharted territory with a record low 182nd bond yield of 2.35 percent.
"This will be a crucial week for the global rally," said Knuthsen. "If the U.S. non-farm payrolls and the German GDP are slightly too strong there could be a correction."
German third quarter gross domestic product figures were scheduled for release on Wednesday, while U.S. November non-farm payrolls data were due on Friday.
Analysts said the recent sharp upmove in prices has gone too far in too short a time to be categorised simply as a traditional year-end rally for bond markets.

"Until last week, the market thought German rates were on hold for the forseeable future," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London. "There was a shift to thinking that rates could come down a bit further to aid growth and keep the EMU bandwagon rolling."

But he said further potential for a fall in German interest rates was limited, as they were already at historic lows. The repo rate is at 3.0 percent, while the lombard and discount rates are at 4.5 percent and 2.5 percent respectively.

Analysts said recent remarks from some Bank of France policymakers suggested pressure on the Bundesbank to cut interest rates was increasing -- but the Bundesbank was unlikely to cave in. Two French central bank council members called for a stronger dollar last week.

"The Bundesbank will probably pursue the route of hinting at rate cuts and a stronger dollar and generally talking expectations up," said Wattret. "But the GDP figures, coupled with strong M3 will not really be conducive to a rate cut."
He said the numbers could be a trigger for a bond market correction.
Sheltering from a bond market storm could prove difficult, analysts said, as most markets have been caught up with the move.

Analysts said gilts, which have underperformed, are risky in the short term, with some expectations of a quarter percentage point rise in British base rates in the first three months of 1997. Base rates are currently at 6.00 percent.
"On a six to 12 month view, gilts look attractive," said Wattret. "It could be one of the markets hit least hard."
Tyson said Swedish bonds had experienced less significant yield convergence than Italy and Spain, and the prospect of lower interest rates and weak growth in Sweden would also underpin that market.
